sections.heading: Coming to you with the weight of conflict
sections.text: Merciful God, when I hear about painful conflict and unpleasant things among your people, it weighs me down. I bring that heaviness to you instead of carrying it alone. I do not want bitterness, defensiveness, or discouragement to take over my heart. Help me come to you honestly with my distress and let you teach me through it.
theological_themes: God invites his people to bring sorrow and distress to him.
Conflict among Christians is grievous because the church belongs to Christ.
The right response to spiritual burden is prayerful dependence, not self-protective anger.

scripture_references.connection: This psalm calls God’s people to pour out their hearts before him because he is their refuge. That grounds the movement of bringing distress over church conflict directly to God.
Paul urges believers to walk with humility, patience, and eagerness to maintain unity. The prayer’s grief over discord among Christians fits that biblical concern for the church’s peace.

sections.heading: Learning to receive correction without defending myself
sections.text: Teach me how to receive correction from friends, even when I feel misunderstood or think I did not deserve it. Use their words to make me more careful about sin, more watchful over my own heart, and more serious about living in a way that does not bring dishonor to you. Let criticism make me examine myself instead of simply protecting my reputation.
theological_themes: Reproof can be a gift when it leads to humility and self-examination.
Even imperfect correction can expose pride and awaken watchfulness against sin.
A believer’s concern is not merely being thought well of, but living faithfully before God.

scripture_references.connection: Proverbs treats faithful correction from a friend as a form of love, even when it wounds. That directly supports asking God for grace to receive reproof rather than reject it defensively.
David asks God to search him and expose any grievous way in him. This gives biblical shape to the prayer’s desire for reproof to lead to honest self-examination before God.
Hebrews teaches that God’s discipline is painful at the time but intended for holiness and righteousness. The prayer asks to interpret correction as one of God’s means of spiritual growth.

sections.heading: Seeing myself rightly before you and others
sections.text: Lord, let correction show me where I lack real spiritual life. Bring me low where I have been proud. Help me stop thinking of myself as important, impressive, or necessary. If others see my weakness, let it make them depend less on me and pray for me more rightly. I am not the foundation of anything good. You are.
theological_themes: True humility refuses self-importance and acknowledges dependence on God.
Human weakness should move others to prayer, not to misplaced trust in a person.
God opposes pride and gives grace to the humble.

scripture_references.connection: Paul warns believers not to think of themselves more highly than they ought, but to think with sober judgment. This supports the prayer’s desire to be stripped of exaggerated self-importance.
Jesus teaches that apart from him his disciples can do nothing. That grounds the confession that the believer is not spiritually self-sufficient or worthy of anyone’s ultimate dependence.
James calls proud sinners to humble themselves before the Lord, trusting that God gives grace to the lowly. This passage fits the prayer’s request that pride be brought down for the soul’s good.

sections.heading: Being content to receive everything from your hand
sections.text: There is a strange sweetness in being nothing before you, owning nothing as if it were mine, and receiving even crumbs from your hand as mercy. Thank you for whatever you give in this life. If it comes from you, it is not beneath me. If it humbles me, it can still be kindness.
theological_themes: Humility finds contentment in receiving from God rather than claiming rights before him.
God’s providence can turn humbling circumstances into spiritual good.

scripture_references.connection: The Canaanite woman accepts the image of crumbs and still trusts Christ’s mercy. That passage illuminates the prayer’s concrete language of being glad to receive even the smallest mercy from God’s hand.
Paul reminds the church that everything they have is received, not self-generated. This supports the prayer’s posture of owning nothing as a basis for pride and receiving all as gift.
Paul teaches that God works all things for the good of those who love him. This supports the prayer’s confidence that even painful reproofs and humbling experiences can be used by God for good.

sections.heading: Clinging to the sweetness of life with you
sections.text: How do people live without you? Where do they go when they are helpless and have no God to call on? How do they bear life without the power of your love drawing them in, and without the sweetness of fellowship with you? Father, keep drawing my desires and affections toward you until my heart finds its center in you.
theological_themes: Life without God is spiritually helpless and empty.
God’s love draws and constrains the believer’s heart.
Communion with God is a real sweetness, not merely a doctrine.

scripture_references.connection: Paul describes the love of Christ as controlling or compelling believers to live for him. That supports the prayer’s language of God’s love drawing and governing the heart.
The psalmist confesses that God is his deepest desire and portion even when body and heart fail. This passage grounds the prayer’s longing for all desires to center on God.
John describes Christian fellowship as participation in fellowship with the Father and the Son. That gives biblical grounding to the prayer’s language of communion with God as a real joy.

sections.heading: Receiving reproof as your loving work in me
sections.text: Give me a living, awake faith—not a dull or lifeless religion. When people correct me, help me receive what is true as coming under your wise hand. Even when the correction is mixed, painful, or unfair, teach me to look for what you may be exposing in me. Let me thank you for any reproof that serves your loving purpose, because I need my pride broken and my soul made healthy before you.
theological_themes: God can use human correction, even imperfect correction, as a means of grace.
The believer should seek God’s glory in humbling circumstances.
Pride must be destroyed because it resists God and harms the soul.

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist treats the rebuke of the righteous as a kindness rather than an injury. This closely supports the prayer’s request to receive correction as spiritually beneficial.

Peter calls believers to clothe themselves with humility and cast their anxieties on God, because God cares for them. This supports both the humbling of pride and the confidence that God’s hand is loving, not cruel.
Proverbs sharply contrasts love of discipline with hatred of reproof. It supports the prayer’s desire for a heart that does not despise correction but receives it as part of wisdom.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original’s language about being “little, mean, and vile,” “nothing,” and “less than nothing” reflects strong Puritan self-abasement. I preserved the intended humility and sin-awareness while avoiding wording that could imply denial of the believer’s God-given dignity as a person made in God’s image and redeemed in Christ.

The request to take reproofs from other people “as from thy hands” could be misused to require passive acceptance of false, manipulative, or abusive criticism. I rendered it with the nuance that God may use even mixed or unfair correction, while the believer receives what is true and looks for God’s sanctifying purpose.

The prayer assumes that public awareness of the speaker’s weakness can be spiritually beneficial because it prevents misplaced dependence on the person. I kept this, but expressed it as a desire that others pray rightly and depend on God rather than as a wish for humiliation for its own sake.
significant_interpretive_choices: “Disagreeable things amongst Christians” was interpreted as painful conflict or discord among believers, not merely unpleasant news in general, because the phrase is tied to burden over the Christian community.
“Want of spirituality” was rendered as lacking real spiritual life or vitality, not as absence of salvation, because the prayer is spoken by a believer asking for sanctifying correction.

“Fed with crumbs from thy hands” was kept as a concrete image of humble dependence on mercy, with Matthew 15:21-28 used as an illuminating biblical connection rather than as a claim that the original directly quotes that passage.
“Vivacity in religion” was interpreted as living, awake faith rather than emotional intensity alone, because the requested result is humble, God-glorifying reception of reproof.
